claim: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during post-learning sleep enhances motor memory consolidation.
source: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during post-learning sleep is known to enhance motor memory consolidation but the underlying neurophysiological processes remain unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The underlying neurophysiological processes of TMR-enhanced motor memory consolidation remain unclear.
source: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during post-learning sleep is known to enhance motor memory consolidation but the underlying neurophysiological processes remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Auditory TMR enhanced slow wave (SW) characteristics.
source: At the neural level, TMR enhanced slow wave (SW) characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Greater TMR-related phase-amplitude coupling between slow (0.5–2 Hz) and sigma (12–16 Hz) oscillations after the SW peak was related to higher TMR effect on performance.
source: Additionally, greater TMR-related phase-amplitude coupling between slow (0.5–2 Hz) and sigma (12–16 Hz) oscillations after the SW peak was related to higher TMR effect on performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analyses between neural measures and behavioral outcomes presented in the study.

claim: Sounds that were not associated to learning strengthened SW-sigma coupling at the SW trough.
source: Importantly, sounds that were not associated to learning strengthened SW-sigma coupling at the SW trough.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing associated and unassociated sounds.

claim: The increase in sigma power nested in the trough of the potential evoked by the unassociated sounds was related to the TMR benefit.
source: Moreover, the increase in sigma power nested in the trough of the potential evoked by the unassociated sounds was related to the TMR benefit.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analyses between neural responses to unassociated sounds and behavioral TMR effects.

claim: Slow and sigma oscillations play a crucial role in either memory reinstatement or protection against irrelevant information depending on their precise temporal coordination during post learning sleep.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that, depending on their precise temporal coordination during post learning sleep, slow and sigma oscillations play a crucial role in either memory reinstatement or protection against irrelevant information; two processes that critically contribute to motor memory consolidation.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of results observed in the study.

claim: Motor memory is the capacity that affords the development of a repertoire of motor skills essential for daily life activities such as typing on a keyboard or buttoning a shirt.
source: Motor memory is the capacity that affords the development of a repertoire of motor skills essential for daily life activities such as typing on a keyboard or buttoning a shirt.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: After initial acquisition, a motor memory undergoes consolidation, which is the offline (i.e. without further practice) process by which the acquired memory trace becomes stable and long-lasting.
source: After initial acquisition, a motor memory undergoes consolidation, which is the offline (i.e. without further practice) process by which the acquired memory trace becomes stable and long-lasting (Maquet, 2001; Robertson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research defining consolidation.

claim: Sleep, and non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM) in particular, is thought to offer a privileged window for the consolidation process to occur.
source: Sleep, and non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM) in particular (Albouy et al., 2008; Albouy et al., 2013), is thought to offer a privileged window for the consolidation process to occur (King et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on sleep and memory consolidation.

claim: Slow waves (SW - high amplitude waves in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band) are specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep.
source: The specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep, such as slow waves (SW - high amplitude waves in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band) (Ngo et al., 2013b), thalamo-cortical spindles (short burst of oscillatory activity in the 12–16 Hz sigma band) (Barakat et al., 2013; Ngo et al., 2019) and hippocampal ripples (80–100 Hz oscillations in humans) (Axmacher et al., 2008), as well as their precise synchrony, have been described to support neuroplasticity processes underlying consolidation (Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research characterizing NREM sleep oscillations.

claim: Thalamo-cortical spindles (short burst of oscillatory activity in the 12–16 Hz sigma band) are specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep.
source: The specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep, such as slow waves (SW - high amplitude waves in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band) (Ngo et al., 2013b), thalamo-cortical spindles (short burst of oscillatory activity in the 12–16 Hz sigma band) (Barakat et al., 2013; Ngo et al., 2019) and hippocampal ripples (80–100 Hz oscillations in humans) (Axmacher et al., 2008), as well as their precise synchrony, have been described to support neuroplasticity processes underlying consolidation (Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research characterizing NREM sleep oscillations.

claim: Hippocampal ripples (80–100 Hz oscillations in humans) are specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep.
source: The specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep, such as slow waves (SW - high amplitude waves in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band) (Ngo et al., 2013b), thalamo-cortical spindles (short burst of oscillatory activity in the 12–16 Hz sigma band) (Barakat et al., 2013; Ngo et al., 2019) and hippocampal ripples (80–100 Hz oscillations in humans) (Axmacher et al., 2008), as well as their precise synchrony, have been described to support neuroplasticity processes underlying consolidation (Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research characterizing NREM sleep oscillations.

claim: The precise synchrony of slow waves, thalamo-cortical spindles, and hippocampal ripples has been described to support neuroplasticity processes underlying consolidation.
source: The specific electrophysiological events characterizing NREM sleep, such as slow waves (SW - high amplitude waves in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band) (Ngo et al., 2013b), thalamo-cortical spindles (short burst of oscillatory activity in the 12–16 Hz sigma band) (Barakat et al., 2013; Ngo et al., 2019) and hippocampal ripples (80–100 Hz oscillations in humans) (Axmacher et al., 2008), as well as their precise synchrony, have been described to support neuroplasticity processes underlying consolidation (Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the role of oscillation synchrony in consolidation.

claim: There has been increasing evidence in both the declarative and motor memory domains that consolidation processes can be augmented by targeted memory reactivation (TMR) applied during post-learning sleep.
source: In recent years, there has been increasing evidence in both the declarative and motor memory domains that consolidation processes can be augmented by experimental interventions such as targeted memory reactivation (TMR) applied during post-learning sleep (Rudoy et al., 2009; Cousins et al., 2016; Schönauer et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies demonstrating TMR effects.

claim: In TMR protocols, sensory stimuli (e.g. sounds) that are associated to the learned material during the learning episode are presented offline, during the consolidation interval, in order to reactivate the encoded memory trace.
source: In TMR protocols, sensory stimuli (e.g. sounds) that are associated to the learned material during the learning episode are presented offline, during the consolidation interval, in order to reactivate the encoded memory trace (Ngo et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a description of the TMR methodology supported by citation.

claim: Memory reinstatement in TMR is thought to be supported by a TMR-mediated reinforcement of the endogenous brain reactivation patterns that occur spontaneously during the consolidation process.
source: This memory reinstatement is thought to be supported by a TMR-mediated reinforcement of the endogenous brain reactivation patterns that occur spontaneously during the consolidation process.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the mechanism of TMR based on existing models.

claim: Reactivations during consolidation are thought to support the transfer of memory traces to the neocortex.
source: Such reactivations are thought to support the transfer of memory traces to the neocortex (Born and Wilhelm, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: The beneficial effect of TMR on motor performance has been highlighted in previous research.
source: While the beneficial effect of TMR on motor performance has been highlighted in previous research (e.g. Antony et al., 2012 ; Faul et al., 2007; Schönauer et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016), the neurophysiological processes supporting these effects have been scarcely studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing TMR benefits on motor performance.

claim: The neurophysiological processes supporting TMR effects on motor performance have been scarcely studied.
source: While the beneficial effect of TMR on motor performance has been highlighted in previous research (e.g. Antony et al., 2012 ; Faul et al., 2007; Schönauer et al., 2014; Cousins et al., 2016), the neurophysiological processes supporting these effects have been scarcely studied.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: The goal of the present study was to elucidate the neurophysiological processes supporting memory reactivation during sleep which underlie TMR-induced enhancement in motor memory consolidation.
source: Therefore, the goal of the present study was to elucidate the neurophysiological processes supporting memory reactivation during sleep which underlie TMR-induced enhancement in motor memory consolidation.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of the study's objective.

claim: Young healthy participants were trained on a Serial Reaction Time task during which they learned two different motor sequences, each associated to a particular sound.
source: Young healthy participants were trained on a Serial Reaction Time task (Nissen and Bullemer, 1987 ) during which they learned two different motor sequences, each associated to a particular sound.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Participants were offered a 90-min nap that was monitored with polysomnography.
source: Participants were then offered a 90-min nap that was monitored with polysomnography.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: During NREM 2–3 sleep stages, the sound associated to one of the two trained sequences ('Associated' sound to the 'Reactivated' sequence) as well as a control sound ('Unassociated') that was not associated to the learned material were played.
source: During NREM 2–3 sleep stages, the sound associated to one of the two trained sequences ('Associated' sound to the 'Reactivated' sequence) as well as a control sound ('Unassociated') that was not associated to the learned material were played.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation during sleep.

claim: The sound associated to the other learned sequence was not presented during the nap, thus serving as a no-reactivation control condition ('Non-reactivated').
source: The sound associated to the other learned sequence was not presented during the nap, thus serving as a no-reactivation control condition ('Non-reactivated').
evidence: This describes the control condition in the experimental design.

claim: The time course of the TMR-induced consolidation process was assessed with retests after the nap episode as well as after a night of sleep spent at home.
source: The time course of the TMR-induced consolidation process was assessed with retests after the nap episode as well as after a night of sleep spent at home.
evidence: This describes the behavioral testing schedule.

claim: Results demonstrated the expected TMR benefit at the behavioral level.
source: At the behavioral level, results demonstrated the expected TMR benefit.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral findings.

claim: TMR mediated enhancement of SWs and SW-sigma coupling after the peak of the SW such that the higher the coupling, the greater the effect of TMR on motor performance.
source: At the brain level, they indicate a TMR-mediated enhancement of SWs and SW-sigma coupling after the peak of the SW such that the higher the coupling, the greater the effect of TMR on motor performance.
evidence: This summarizes the neural findings related to associated sounds.

claim: Unassociated sounds strengthened SW-sigma coupling at a different phase of the SW (trough).
source: Intriguingly, unassociated sounds also strengthened SW-sigma coupling but at a different phase of the SW (trough) and the increase in sigma power nested in the trough of the potential evoked by the unassociated sounds was related to the TMR benefit.
evidence: This summarizes the neural findings related to unassociated sounds.

claim: Sigma oscillations may play a dual role in the consolidation process depending on both the nature of the information to be processed and the phase of the slow oscillation in which they occur.
source: Altogether, our findings suggest that sigma oscillations may play a dual role in the consolidation process depending on both the nature of the information to be processed and the phase of the slow oscillation in which they occur.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of results.

claim: Participants learned the two sequence conditions (reactivated and non-reactivated sequences) to a similar extent during initial learning.
source: Analyses of the pre-nap training data indicated that participants learned the two sequence conditions (reactivated and non-reactivated sequences) to a similar extent during initial learning (16 blocks of training; main effect of Block: F(15, 345)=34.82; p-value = 2.04e-26; η²=0.6; main effect of Condition: F(1, 23)=0.16; p-value = 0.69; Block by Condition interaction: F(15, 345)=1.09; p-value = 0.37; Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Performance reached similar levels between conditions during the pre-nap test session.
source: Results showed that while performance reached similar levels between conditions (4 blocks; main effect of Condition: F(1,23) = 3.39e-5; p-value = 0.99; Block by Condition interaction: F(3,69) = 1.21; p-value = 0.31), asymptotic performance levels were not reached as shown by a significant Block effect (F(3,69) = 6.67; p-value = 0.001; η²=0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Asymptotic performance levels were not reached during the initial pre-nap test session as shown by a significant Block effect.
source: Results showed that while performance reached similar levels between conditions (4 blocks; main effect of Condition: F(1,23) = 3.39e-5; p-value = 0.99; Block by Condition interaction: F(3,69) = 1.21; p-value = 0.31), asymptotic performance levels were not reached as shown by a significant Block effect (F(3,69) = 6.67; p-value = 0.001; η²=0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing continued improvement across blocks.

claim: After removing the first block of the pre-nap test session, performance on remaining blocks was stable.
source: To meet the performance plateau pre-requisite to compute offline changes in performance, the first block of the pre-nap test session driving this effect was removed from further analyses. Performance on remaining blocks was stable as indicated by a non-significant Block effect (F(2,46) = 1.56; p-value = 0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis after data exclusion.

claim: A performance plateau was ultimately reached and both sequence conditions were learned similarly.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that a performance plateau was ultimately reached and both sequence conditions were learned similarly (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the statistical analyses and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Changes in performance were significantly higher at the post-night as compared to the post-nap retest.
source: A repeated measures analysis of variance (rmANOVA) performed on offline changes in performance with Time-point (post-nap vs. post-night) and Condition (reactivated vs. non-reactivated) as within-subject factors showed a significant Time-point effect, whereby changes in performance were significantly higher at the post-night as compared to the post-nap retest (F(1,23) = 46.53; p-value = 5.89e-7; η²=0.67; Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Offline changes in performance for the reactivated sequence were significantly higher than for the non-reactivated sequence.
source: Critically, offline changes in performance for the reactivated sequence were significantly higher than for the non-reactivated sequence (Condition effect: F(1,23) = 4.75; p-value = 0.0397; η²=0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing the TMR effect.

claim: The Condition by Time-point interaction was not significant for offline changes in performance.
source: The Condition by Time-point interaction was not significant (F(1,23) = 7.42e-4; p-value = 0.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Behavioral results indicate a TMR-induced enhancement in performance that did not differ across nap and night intervals.
source: In conclusion, our behavioral results indicate a TMR-induced enhancement in performance that did not differ across nap and night intervals.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral findings.

claim: All the participants slept during the nap (average total sleep time: 67 min; average sleep efficiency: 74.9%).
source: Briefly, results indicate that all the participants slept during the nap (average total sleep time: 67 min; average sleep efficiency: 74.9%) and that cues were accurately presented in NREM sleep (average stimulation accuracy: 88.4%).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysomnographic data.

claim: Cues were accurately presented in NREM sleep (average stimulation accuracy: 88.4%).
source: Briefly, results indicate that all the participants slept during the nap (average total sleep time: 67 min; average sleep efficiency: 74.9%) and that cues were accurately presented in NREM sleep (average stimulation accuracy: 88.4%).
evidence: This claim is supported by monitoring data during the experiment.

claim: The amplitude of the ERP trough was significantly deeper following associated as compared to unassociated cues.
source: Between-condition comparisons using Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that the amplitude of the ERP trough was significantly deeper (V=75, p-value = 0.016) following associated as compared to unassociated cues (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: Both peak-to-peak (PTP) amplitude and density of detected SWs (averaged across all EEG channels) were greater for the associated as compared to the unassociated stimulation intervals.
source: Concerning the detected SWs (Figure 4a), both peak-to-peak (PTP) amplitude and density (averaged across all EEG channels) were greater for the associated as compared to the unassociated stimulation intervals (amplitude: t=2.7; df = 21; p-value = 0.009; Cohen's d=0.55; and density V=197; p-value = 0.01; r=0.58).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of detected slow waves and reference to Figure 4a.

claim: SW PTP amplitude did not differ between rest intervals and the two types of stimulation intervals.
source: Exploratory analyses including the detected SWs in the non-stimulation (rest) intervals did not highlight PTP amplitude differences between the rest intervals and the two types of stimulation intervals (rest vs. associated: t=0.82; df = 21; p-value = 0.42; rest vs. unassociated: t=–0.92; df = 21; p-value = 0.42; Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing rest and stimulation conditions.

claim: SW density was significantly lower during the rest as compared to the stimulation intervals, regardless of the cue type.
source: However, SW density was significantly lower during the rest as compared to the stimulation intervals, regardless of the cue type (rest vs. associated: V=232; p-uncorrected=0.0002; p-FDR=0.0004; r=0.66; rest vs. unassociated: V=224; p- uncorrected = 0.0008; p-FDR=0.00081; r=0.6; Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Auditory stimulation induced an overall increase in SW density.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that auditory stimulation induced an overall increase in SW density, and, more importantly, that the associated sounds resulted in an increase in SW amplitude and density as compared to the unassociated sounds.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the SW findings.

claim: Associated sounds resulted in an increase in SW amplitude and density as compared to the unassociated sounds.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that auditory stimulation induced an overall increase in SW density, and, more importantly, that the associated sounds resulted in an increase in SW amplitude and density as compared to the unassociated sounds.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the SW findings.

claim: Sleep spindle density averaged across all channels did not differ between associated and unassociated stimulation intervals.
source: Sleep spindle density averaged across all channels did not differ between associated and unassociated stimulation intervals (V=98, p-value = 0.89).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spindle data.

claim: Additional spindle features including amplitude and frequency did not yield any significant differences between stimulation conditions.
source: Similarly, exploratory analyses on additional spindle features including amplitude and frequency did not yield any significant differences between stimulation conditions (all p-values > 0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Spindle density did not differ between stimulation and rest intervals.
source: Results show that spindle density did not differ between stimulation and rest intervals (V=97, p-value = 0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing stimulation and rest conditions.

claim: The difference in spindle amplitude was marginally significant with higher amplitudes during the auditory stimulation intervals as compared to the rest intervals.
source: Interestingly, the difference in spindle amplitude was marginally significant with higher amplitudes during the auditory stimulation intervals as compared to the rest intervals (V=199; p-value = 0.065; r=0.73), whereas spindle frequency showed the opposite pattern (t=–3.42; df = 22; p-value = 0.005; Cohen's d=0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing a trend.

claim: Spindle frequency was lower during stimulation as compared to rest intervals.
source: Interestingly, the difference in spindle amplitude was marginally significant with higher amplitudes during the auditory stimulation intervals as compared to the rest intervals (V=199; p-value = 0.065; r=0.73), whereas spindle frequency showed the opposite pattern (t=–3.42; df = 22; p-value = 0.005; Cohen's d=0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: While auditory stimulation altered spindle features (frequency and amplitude to a lesser extent) as compared to rest, the two sound conditions did not differently influence these characteristics.
source: In summary, these results indicate that while auditory stimulation altered spindle features (frequency and amplitude to a lesser extent) as compared to rest, the two sound conditions did not differently influence these characteristics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the spindle findings.

claim: The CBP test on auditory cue-locked ERPAC values did not highlight any significant clusters between the two stimulation conditions.
source: The ERPAC values locked to the auditory cues were compared between the two stimulation conditions. The CBP test did not highlight any significant clusters (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster p-value = 0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The preferred coupling phase locked to auditory cues did not significantly differ between conditions.
source: The preferred coupling phase, which represents the phase at which the maximum amplitude is observed, did not significantly differ between conditions (F(1,46) = 0.3, p-value = 0.9).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The stimulation conditions did not influence the coupling between the phase of the slow oscillations and the amplitude of sigma oscillations at the auditory cue.
source: These results suggest that the stimulation conditions did not influence the coupling between the phase of the slow oscillations and the amplitude of sigma oscillations at the auditory cue.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the cue-locked PAC findings.

claim: The coupling between the phase of the signal in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band and the amplitude of the signal in the 14–18 Hz frequency band was significantly stronger around the negative SW peak during unassociated as compared to associated stimulation intervals.
source: Comparison of the ERPAC locked to the negative peak of the SWs (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 for channel level data) between stimulation conditions revealed a significant cluster (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster p-value = 0.024; Cohen's d=–0.56). Specifically, the coupling between the phase of the signal in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band and the amplitude of the signal in the 14–18 Hz frequency band was significantly stronger around the negative SW peak (from –0.8 to 0.2 s relative to negative peak) during unassociated as compared to associated stimulation intervals (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6.

claim: A significant cluster was observed in SW-locked ERPAC between unassociated stimulation and rest.
source: The exploratory comparison between rest and associated stimulation intervals did not reveal any significant clusters (alpha threshold = 0.025, all cluster p-values > 0.6) but a significant cluster was observed between unassociated stimulation and rest (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster p-value = 0.001; Cohen's d=0.53; Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6c.

claim: The preferred phases in each of the conditions (associated, unassociated, rest) were not significantly different for SW-locked ERPAC.
source: The preferred phases in each of the conditions were not significantly different (associated vs. unassociated: F(1,42) = 0;007, p-value = 0.94; associated vs. rest: F(1,42) = 0.01, p-value = 0.91; unassociated vs. rest: F(1,42) = 0.3, p-value = 0.87; see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Slow and sigma oscillation coupling observed just before the onset of the SW was stronger during unassociated as compared to associated and rest intervals but the preferred coupling phase was not modulated by the experimental conditions.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that slowand sigma oscillation coupling observed just before the onset of the SW was stronger during unassociated as compared to associated and rest intervals but that the preferred coupling phase was not modulated by the experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the SW-locked PAC findings.

claim: Correlation analyses between the TMR index and the density of SW and spindles as well as with the amplitude of the ERP did not yield any significant results.
source: Correlation analyses between the TMR index (i.e. the difference in offline changes in performance – averaged across time points – between the reactivated and the non-reactivated sequence) and the density of SW and spindles as well as with the amplitude of the ERP did not yield any significant results (density of spontaneous SW: S=2486, p-value = 0.97) density of spontaneous spindles S=1412, p-value = 0.24; amplitude of the negative peak of the ERP S=2282, p-value = 0.73.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The correlational CBP analysis between the TMR index and the difference in TF power elicited by the different auditory cues highlighted one significant cluster.
source: However, the correlational CBP analysis between the TMR index and the difference in TF power elicited by the different auditory cues highlighted one significant cluster (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster centered on 0.5 s post-cue p-value = 0.022, rho = - 0.46; Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for channel level data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7a.

claim: Higher TMR index (i.e. greater behavioral benefit of TMR) was related to higher sigma oscillation power for the unassociated compared to the associated sound condition.
source: The resulting scatter plot presented in Figure 7b indicates that higher TMR index (i.e. greater behavioral benefit of TMR) was related to higher sigma oscillation power for the unassociated compared to the associated sound condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis and reference to Figure 7b.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between the auditory-locked ERPAC metrics and the TMR index.
source: Finally, with respect to ERPAC-TMR index correlation analyses, no significant correlation was observed between the auditory-locked ERPAC metrics and the TMR index (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster p-values >0.09).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The associated vs. unassociated difference in coupling strength between the phase of the signal in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band and the amplitude of the signal in the 14.5–17 Hz frequency band, just after the SW peak (0.5 and 1 s), was positively correlated with the TMR index.
source: In contrast, cluster-based permutation correlational tests performed between the 12 and 16 Hz TFR SW-locked ERPAC difference between the two conditions and the TMR index revealed a significant cluster. Results show that the associated vs. unassociated difference in coupling strength between the phase of the signal in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band and the amplitude of the signal in the 14.5–17 Hz frequency band, just after the SW peak (0.5 and 1 s), was positively correlated with the TMR index (alpha threshold = 0.025, cluster p-value = 0.0499, rho = 0.55; Figure 8a and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for channel level data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 8a.

claim: The stronger the phase-amplitude coupling during associated as compared to the unassociated stimulation intervals, the higher the TMR index.
source: The resulting scatter plot (Figure 8b) indicates that the stronger the phase-amplitude coupling during associated as compared to the unassociated stimulation intervals, the higher the TMR index.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis and reference to Figure 8b.

claim: The current results demonstrate a TMR-induced behavioral advantage such that offline changes in performance were larger on the reactivated as compared to the non-reactivated sequence.
source: In the present study, we examined the impact of auditory TMR on motor memory consolidation as well as the neurophysiological processes supporting reactivation during sleep. Our results demonstrate a TMR-induced behavioral advantage such that offline changes in performance were larger on the reactivated as compared to the non-reactivated sequence.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main behavioral finding.

claim: The behavioral results are in line with earlier motor learning studies showing improvement in performance after auditory or olfactory TMR during sleep.
source: These behavioral results are in line with earlier motor learning studies showing improvement in performance after auditory (Schönauer et al., 2014; Antony et al., 2012; Cousins et al., 2016) or olfactory (Laventure et al., 2016) TMR during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The current results suggest that TMR-induced consolidation is not a protracted process that needs additional time and/or sleep to develop, as a behavioral advantage could already be observed immediately after the TMR episode.
source: As opposed to earlier TMR research though, the current results suggest that TMR-induced consolidation is not a protracted process that needs additional time and/or sleep to develop (Cairney et al., 2018), as a behavioral advantage could already be observed immediately after the TMR episode.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the timing of the observed TMR effect.

claim: In contrast to earlier work showing that TMR effects can be transient, the current data indicate that the effect of TMR on motor performance was sustained overnight.
source: Also, in contrast to earlier work showing that TMR effects can be transient (Cousins et al., 2016), the current data indicate that the effect of TMR on motor performance was sustained overnight.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the persistence of the TMR effect.

claim: It remains unclear whether discrepancies with earlier work are related to the nature of the task (e.g. declarative vs. motor), the sensory stimulus used for reactivation (words vs. sound) or the duration of the reactivation / sleeping episode (nap vs. night).
source: It remains unclear whether these discrepancies are related to the nature of the task (e.g. declarative vs. motor), the sensory stimulus used for reactivation (words vs. sound) or the duration of the reactivation / sleeping episode (nap vs. night).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for differences with prior work.

claim: The findings suggest that the TMR episode during a nap immediately following learning set the reactivated memory trace on a distinct yet parallel trajectory as compared to the non-reactivated memory trace.
source: Nevertheless, our findings suggest that the TMR episode during a nap immediately following learning set the reactivated memory trace on a distinct yet parallel trajectory as compared to the non-reactivated memory trace.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: The amplitude of the negative component of the auditory ERP was higher for the sounds associated to the motor memory task as compared to the unassociated sounds.
source: TMR effects were also observed at the brain level such that electrophysiological responses differed according to whether they were evoked by associated or unassociated cues. Specifically, the amplitude of the negative component of the auditory ERP was higher for the sounds associated to the motor memory task as compared to the unassociated sounds.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the ERP findings.

claim: The ERP results are in line with findings from earlier associative learning studies performed during wakefulness showing that auditory cues evoke larger responses after conditioning.
source: These results are in line with findings from earlier associative learning studies performed during wakefulness showing that auditory cues evoke larger responses after conditioning (i.e. after they are associated to another stimulus) and that ERP amplitude is restored to pre-association levels after extinction (see Christoffersen and Schachtman, 2016 for a review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of prior research.

claim: The current findings extend prior observation of a modulation of auditory-TMR-evoked responses during sleep.
source: The current findings also extend prior observation of a modulation of auditory-TMR-evoked responses during sleep (Rudoy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An earlier study showed that auditory cues presented during post-learning sleep evoked larger ERPs when they were associated to items better remembered at subsequent recall as compared to cues associated to less remembered items.
source: This earlier study showed that auditory cues presented during post-learning sleep evoked larger ERPs when they were associated to items better remembered at subsequent recall as compared to cues associated to less remembered items.
evidence: This is a description of findings from prior research.

claim: The current findings provide the first direct evidence of an ERP modulation based on the memory content of the cue during post-learning sleep.
source: Our findings not only concur with this post-hoc analysis, but also provide the first direct evidence of an ERP modulation based on the memory content of the cue during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The difference in brain potentials during sleep might be seen as the neural signature of the plasticity processes that occurred during learning.
source: This difference in brain potentials during sleep might be seen as the neural signature of the plasticity processes that occurred during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ERP findings.

claim: The ERP effects might also be attributed to the (re)processing of the memory trace during post-learning sleep.
source: Not exclusive to the previous speculation, such effects might also be attributed to the (re)processing of the memory trace during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the ERP findings.

claim: The difference in ERP amplitude observed in the present study is unlikely to be due to familiarity effects, as new or rare auditory stimuli usually present larger negative amplitudes as compared to old or frequent sounds during both sleep and wakefulness.
source: One could argue that the difference in ERP amplitude observed in the present study might be due to familiarity effects, as the unassociated sound might have been perceived as novel as compared to the associated sound. We argue that this is unlikely as new or rare auditory stimuli usually present larger negative amplitudes as compared to old or frequent sounds during both sleep and wakefulness (e.g. FN 400 [Rugg and Curran, 2007; Paller et al., 2012]) for old/new paradigms during wake and mismatch negativity components for oddball paradigms during both wake and sleep (Näätänen et al., 2007; Ruby et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ERP components.

claim: The auditory evoked brain responses observed in the current study reflect the (re)processing of the motor memory trace that was encoded during initial learning.
source: Instead, we propose that the auditory evoked brain responses observed in the current study reflect the (re)processing of the motor memory trace that was encoded during initial learning.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the meaning of the ERP findings.

claim: The negative peak of the potential evoked by the unassociated cues was not only lower (i.e. less negative) than for the associated cues but was also sometimes even absent on some channels.
source: It is worth noting that the negative peak of the potential evoked by the unassociated cues was not only lower (i.e. less negative) than for the associated cues but was also sometimes even absent on some channels (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of the data and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The observations about unassociated cue ERPs are partly in line with earlier research but contradict other findings.
source: These observations are partly in line with earlier research (Cairney et al., 2018) but contradict other findings. For example, Weigenand et al., 2016 as well as Schreiner and Rasch, 2015 observed significant negative responses evoked by control sounds or by sounds that were associated to later forgotten items.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Discrepancies with prior work remain unclear but might in part be explained by methodological differences that are known to influence the amplitude of ERPs.
source: These discrepancies remain unclear but might in part be explained by methodological differences that are known to influence the amplitude of ERPs (e.g. sleep cycle stimulated, electrode(s) examined, number of stimulation repetitions provided).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for differences with prior work.

claim: SW density was higher during sound presentation as compared to rest.
source: In addition to the modulation of auditory-evoked responses described above, the properties of the detected (spontaneous) SWs were influenced by sound presentation and sound condition. Specifically, SW density was higher during sound presentation as compared to rest and the density and amplitude of the SWs were greater during intervals of associated – as compared to unassociated – cue stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the SW findings.

claim: The density and amplitude of the SWs were greater during intervals of associated – as compared to unassociated – cue stimulation.
source: In addition to the modulation of auditory-evoked responses described above, the properties of the detected (spontaneous) SWs were influenced by sound presentation and sound condition. Specifically, SW density was higher during sound presentation as compared to rest and the density and amplitude of the SWs were greater during intervals of associated – as compared to unassociated – cue stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the SW findings.

claim: The effect of sound presentation on SW characteristics is in line with previous work showing sound-related entrainment of SW trains and increase in SW amplitude during sleep.
source: The effect of sound presentation on SW characteristics is in line with previous work showing sound-related entrainment of SW trains and increase in SW amplitude during sleep (Ngo et al., 2013a; Ngo et al., 2013b; Ngo et al., 2015; Ngo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The data show that the memory content of the cue modulated SW physiology above and beyond the mere effect of sound presentation.
source: More importantly, in line with the ERP results, our data show that the memory content of the cue modulated SW physiology above and beyond the mere effect of sound presentation.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the specificity of the SW modulation.

claim: This is the first evidence, to the best of our knowledge, of a modulation of SW physiology based on the relevance of the sensory cues presented during sleep.
source: This is the first evidence, to the best of our knowledge, of a modulation of SW physiology based on the relevance of the sensory cues presented during sleep.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The processing of the memory content associated to the cue resulted in enhanced SW activity.
source: We speculate that the processing of the memory content associated to the cue resulted in enhanced SW activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SW findings.

claim: The greater amplitude of the SWs during associated sound intervals might reflect neural synchronization known to promote sleep-dependent plasticity processes.
source: Specifically, the greater amplitude of the SWs during associated sound intervals might reflect neural synchronization (Carrier et al., 2011; Esser et al., 2007) known to promote sleep-dependent plasticity processes for example (Born and Wilhelm, 2012; Ngo et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The TMR-effect observed in this study might be mediated by SWs likely in relation with spindle activity.
source: We thus propose that the TMR-effect observed in this study might therefore be mediated by SWs likely in relation with spindle activity.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the mechanism of TMR.

claim: The characteristics of spontaneous spindles (amplitude and frequency) were only modulated by sound presentation and not sound condition.
source: While the characteristics of spontaneous spindles (amplitude and frequency) were only modulated by sound presentation and not sound condition, the properties of sigma oscillations (i.e. its amplitude and its coupling with the SO phase) were differently affected by the cue type and related to the TMR-induced behavioral advantage.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the spindle findings.

claim: The properties of sigma oscillations (i.e. its amplitude and its coupling with the SO phase) were differently affected by the cue type and related to the TMR-induced behavioral advantage.
source: While the characteristics of spontaneous spindles (amplitude and frequency) were only modulated by sound presentation and not sound condition, the properties of sigma oscillations (i.e. its amplitude and its coupling with the SO phase) were differently affected by the cue type and related to the TMR-induced behavioral advantage.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the sigma oscillation findings.

claim: The observation of a modulation of spindle characteristics irrespective of the sound condition suggests that spindle activity (in term of events) during reactivation is not related to motor memory processing per se.
source: The observation of a modulation of spindle characteristics irrespective of the sound condition suggests that spindle activity (in term of events) during reactivation is not related to motor memory processing per se.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the lack of condition-specific spindle effects.

claim: This stands in contrast with earlier reports of spindle-mediated effect of TMR on the consolidation of both declarative and motor memory tasks.
source: This stands in contrast with earlier reports of spindle-mediated effect of TMR on the consolidation of both declarative (Cairney et al., 2018) and motor (Laventure et al., 2016; Cousins et al., 2016) memory tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Earlier work did not compare different stimulus conditions as in the present study.
source: It is worth noting, however, that this earlier work did not compare different stimulus conditions as in the present study.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about differences with prior work.

claim: Previous research demonstrated that reactivation was related to an increase in spindle features (amplitude and frequency) that were linked to the TMR-induced motor performance advantage.
source: Nonetheless, this previous research demonstrated that reactivation was related to an increase in spindle features (amplitude and frequency) that were linked to the TMR-induced motor performance advantage (Laventure et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The results do not rule out the involvement of spindle activity in TMR-related motor memory consolidation processes.
source: Importantly, it is worth explicitly stating that our results do not rule out the involvement of spindle activity in TMR-related motor memory consolidation processes.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Recent evidence has brought forward the idea that spindle event detection in general is less sensitive than the study of the sigma rhythm as a whole.
source: Recent evidence has brought forward the idea that spindle event detection in general is less sensitive than the study of the sigma rhythm as a whole (Dimitrov et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Sigma oscillation properties – as opposed to spindle events – were modulated by the sound condition and such modulation was related to the TMR-induced behavioral advantage.
source: In line with these observations, our results show that sigma oscillation properties – as opposed to spindle events – were modulated by the sound condition and that such modulation was related to the TMR-induced behavioral advantage.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the sigma oscillation findings.

claim: Higher coupling between sigma oscillation amplitude and the SO phase, for associated as compared to unassociated sounds, on the descending phase following the peak of the SW was correlated with the TMR index.
source: Specifically, higher coupling between sigma oscillation amplitude and the SO phase, for associated as compared to unassociated sounds, on the descending phase following the peak of the SW was correlated with the TMR index.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the PAC-behavior correlation findings.

claim: This is the first time that the strength of the coupling between the SO phase and the amplitude of the sigma oscillations nested within the peak of the SW is directly related to a TMR-related behavioral advantage.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the strength of the coupling between the SO phase and the amplitude of the sigma oscillations nested within the peak of the SW is directly related to a TMR-related behavioral advantage.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Earlier studies comparing different age groups provided convincing, yet indirect, evidence that the precise temporal coordination of SO and sleep spindles represents a critical mechanism for sleep-dependent memory consolidation.
source: Earlier studies comparing different age groups provided convincing, yet indirect, evidence that the precise temporal coordination of SO and sleep spindles represents a critical mechanism for sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Muehlroth et al., 2019; Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The timing reported in earlier work is consistent with the current data showing increased SW-sigma coupling on the descending phase following the peak of the SW.
source: The timing reported in this earlier work is consistent with the current data showing increased SW-sigma coupling on the descending phase following the peak of the SW.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with prior research.

claim: The results are in line with previous frameworks proposing that sigma oscillation / spindles offer a privileged time window for relevant memories to be reinstated during sleep.
source: Our results are also in line with previous frameworks proposing that sigma oscillation (Cairney et al., 2018) / spindles (Antony et al., 2019) offer a privileged time window for relevant memories to be reinstated during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Together with evidence that TMR boosted SW features, the current data suggest that both SWs and sigma oscillations play a critical role in the reactivation of motor memories.
source: Together with evidence that TMR boosted SW features, the current data suggest that both SWs and sigma oscillations play a critical role in the reactivation of motor memories.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the findings.

claim: The coupling between sigma amplitude and the SO phase was strengthened for unassociated sounds just before the onset of the SW negative peak.
source: In addition to the modulation of neurophysiological responses described above and triggered by the associated sounds, we report an intriguing pattern of brain results for the unassociated sounds. Specifically, the coupling between sigma amplitude and the SO phase was strengthened for unassociated sounds just before the onset of the SW negative peak.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for unassociated sounds.

claim: The increase in sigma power nested in the trough of the auditory evoked potential for unassociated (as compared to associated) sounds was related to higher TMR-induced performance enhancement.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the increase in sigma power nested in the trough of the auditory evoked potential for unassociated (as compared to associated) sounds was related to higher TMR-induced performance enhancement.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the correlation findings for unassociated sounds.

claim: Sigma oscillations might prevent the processing of unassociated/irrelevant sounds during post-learning sleep which might in turn be reflected by a decrease in the amplitude of the slow electrophysiological responses during non-associated sound intervals.
source: It is tempting to speculate that sigma oscillations might prevent the processing of unassociated/irrelevant sounds during post-learning sleep which might in turn be reflected by a decrease in the amplitude of the slow electrophysiological responses (i.e. smaller ERP and SWs) during non-associated sound intervals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings for unassociated sounds.

claim: Sigma oscillations might play the role of a gatekeeper for the consolidation process and protect the motor memory trace against potential interfering effects induced by the unassociated sounds which might in turn potentiate the effect of TMR at the behavioral level.
source: We argue that sigma oscillations might play the role of a gatekeeper for the consolidation process and protect the motor memory trace against potential interfering effects induced by the unassociated sounds which might in turn potentiate the effect of TMR at the behavioral level.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the functional role of sigma oscillations.

claim: Higher SW-sigma coupling during unassociated stimulation intervals was related to lower SW amplitude and density.
source: Results showed a negative correlation between SW-sigma coupling and SW features such that higher coupling was related to lower SW amplitude and density during unassociated stimulation intervals.
evidence: This claim is supported by exploratory correlational analyses.

claim: These results provide further support for the protective effect of sigma oscillations (nested in the trough of slow oscillations) against potential interfering effects induced by the unassociated sounds.
source: These results provide further support for the protective effect of sigma oscillations (nested in the trough of slow oscillations) against potential interfering effects induced by the unassociated sounds.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the correlation findings.

claim: These assumptions are in line with a growing body of literature pointing towards a sensory gating role of spindle activity / sigma oscillations that might be critical to facilitate the memory consolidation process during sleep.
source: These assumptions are also in line with a growing body of literature pointing towards a sensory gating role of spindle activity / sigma oscillations (Dang-Vu et al., 2011; Schabus et al., 2012) that might be critical to facilitate the memory consolidation process during sleep (Schreiner and Staudigl, 2020; Antony et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It has been proposed that a function of the thalamus is to suppress distraction and gate information processing via alpha/beta oscillations during wakefulness and sigma oscillations during sleep.
source: Specifically, it has been proposed that a function of the thalamus is to suppress distraction and gate information processing via alpha/beta oscillations during wakefulness (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010) and sigma oscillations during sleep (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Further support for the gating hypothesis comes from observations of both increased arousal threshold as well as decreased amplitude of auditory ERP when sounds are presented simultaneously to a spindle event.
source: Further support for the gating hypothesis comes from observations of both increased arousal threshold as well as decreased amplitude of auditory ERP when sounds are presented simultaneously to a spindle event (Yamadori, 1971; Cote et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies using simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings showed that the BOLD responses in relation to sound processing are inconsistent or even absent when sounds occur during sleep spindles or before the negative peak of the SW.
source: Along the same lines, previous studies using simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings showed that the BOLD responses in relation to sound processing are inconsistent or even absent when sounds occur during sleep spindles or before the negative peak of the SW (Dang-Vu et al., 2011; Schabus et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The present data suggest that the precise SO-sigma coordination does not only play a role in the reinstatement of relevant memories, but is also critical to prevent the processing of irrelevant information during post-learning sleep.
source: The present data therefore suggest that the precise SO-sigma coordination does not only play a role in the reinstatement of relevant memories, but is also critical to prevent the processing of irrelevant information during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the findings.

claim: These observations are remarkably in line with recent theoretical views putting forward the concept that temporally precise SO-spindle coupling might not convey only memory-specific information.
source: These observations are remarkably in line with recent theoretical views putting forward the concept that temporally precise SO-spindle coupling might not convey only memory-specific information (Helfrich et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent theoretical paper.

claim: It is argued that while synchronized states might trigger memory reactivation, the underlying neural activity might offer limited opportunities for information processing.
source: It is argued that while synchronized states might trigger memory reactivation, the underlying neural activity might offer limited opportunities for information processing.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical argument from prior work.

claim: The data concur with the theory that SO-sigma coupling, depending on its temporal characteristics, either prevents the processing of irrelevant information or supports memory reactivation during post-learning sleep.
source: Our data concur with this theory as they suggest that SO-sigma coupling, depending on its temporal characteristics, either prevents the processing of irrelevant information or supports memory reactivation during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim linking the findings to existing theory.

claim: The results depict a complex organization of the different physiological processes supporting motor memory consolidation during post-learning sleep.
source: In conclusion, our results depict a complex organization of the different physiological processes supporting motor memory consolidation during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings.

claim: Associated sounds appeared to boost SW features and SO-sigma coupling at the peak of the SW.
source: While associated sounds appeared to boost SW features and SO-sigma coupling at the peak of the SW, unassociated sounds predominantly modulated the properties of the sigma oscillations at the trough of the slow oscillation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for associated sounds.

claim: Unassociated sounds predominantly modulated the properties of the sigma oscillations at the trough of the slow oscillation.
source: While associated sounds appeared to boost SW features and SO-sigma coupling at the peak of the SW, unassociated sounds predominantly modulated the properties of the sigma oscillations at the trough of the slow oscillation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for unassociated sounds.

claim: The findings suggest a dual role of sigma oscillations whereby, depending on their temporal coordination with SWs, they either protect memories against irrelevant material processing or promote the reactivation of relevant motor memories; two processes that critically contribute to the motor memory consolidation process.
source: Our findings suggest a dual role of sigma oscillations whereby, depending on their temporal coordination with SWs, they either protect memories against irrelevant material processing or promote the reactivation of relevant motor memories; two processes that critically contribute to the motor memory consolidation process.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the study.
